approachQuestion.prompt:
Count a reading

Given a read-only nondecreasing random-access integer array a and integer x, return how many entries equal x. Duplicates are allowed. 0 <= n <= 200000. Examples: a=[1,2,2,2,5], x=2 -> 3; a=[], x=4 -> 0; a=[1,3], x=2 -> 0.
constraints: Use only the stated input ordering and access guarantees.

options.text: Iteratively find the first index with value >=x and the first with value >x, treating n as the missing boundary; subtract the two indices.
options.feedback: Two boundaries isolate an equal-value interval; equality search alone loses multiplicity.

options.text: Use binary search to find any match, then walk in both directions until all equal entries have been counted.
options.feedback: The walks are correct, but a run occupying the entire array forces a full traversal.

options.text: Return 1 when ordinary binary search finds x and 0 otherwise.
options.feedback: For [2,2], x=2 the answer is 2, not 1.

feedback.reason: Iteratively find the first index with value >=x and the first with value >x, treating n as the missing boundary; subtract the two indices. Two boundaries isolate an equal-value interval; equality search alone loses multiplicity.
details: Iteratively find the first index with value >=x and the first with value >x, treating n as the missing boundary; subtract the two indices. Two boundaries isolate an equal-value interval; equality search alone loses multiplicity.
Lower and upper bounds bracket all copies of x. Subtracting their indices handles absent x too, because both boundaries then coincide. An arbitrary equality hit cannot determine the multiplicity.

“Iteratively find the first index with value >=x and the first with value >x, treating n as the missing boundary; subtract the two indices.”: Two boundaries isolate an equal-value interval; equality search alone loses multiplicity.
“Use binary search to find any match, then walk in both directions until all equal entries have been counted.”: The walks are correct, but a run occupying the entire array forces a full traversal.
“Return 1 when ordinary binary search finds x and 0 otherwise.”: For [2,2], x=2 the answer is 2, not 1.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For target-method, choose the tightest worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair. n is array length; two iterative bound searches use random access, constant-time comparisons and overflow-safe index arithmetic. No copies or recursion. Input storage and returned result storage are excluded; all temporary buffers and call stacks are included.
constraints: Use worst-case bounds. Count all working memory including any stack; exclude supplied inputs and the scalar result.

feedback.reason: Two independent halving searches retain only scalar boundaries.
details: Each of the lower- and upper-bound searches uses logarithmically many constant-cost probes. Two sequential searches add to O(1+log(n+1)), not a product of logarithms. Reused scalar bounds keep space constant.
“O(log(n + 1) + 1) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: Two boundaries isolate an equal-value interval; equality search alone loses multiplicity.
“O(n*n + 1) time, O(n + 1) auxiliary space”: Two bound searches each halve the interval; neither enumerates position pairs or allocates n-entry state.
“O(1) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: A large equal-value block still requires finding its two boundaries; one constant-time equality check cannot locate both.
